name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once, mean latency: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf (Google.Protobuf, C#) 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x) and vs MessagePack-CSharp 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x). BebopMessage 231.7 ns is ~4.5x faster than Protobuf and ~6.8x faster than MessagePack (ratios derived from page data). The benchmark repo's README says Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization', and that on deserialization Protobuf 'becomes the slowest of the binary serializers'.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.1 DefaultJob (default Release build configuration, X64 RyuJIT), .NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7.21379.14, runtime .NET 5.0.9 (5.0.921.35908). The net5.0 target sets no custom optimization properties in Benchmarks/Benchmarks.csproj. Packages: bebop 2.2.6, Google.Protobuf 3.17.3, MessagePack 2.3.75.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical and 16 physical cores. BenchmarkDotNet reports the OS as Windows 10.0.22449.
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: All numbers are C#: Bebop 2.2.6 vs the C# Protobuf (Google.Protobuf 3.17.3) and MessagePack-CSharp 2.3.75 runtimes on .NET 5.0.9, run in 2021. Bebop is now at v3.2.3 (2025-09-16) and .NET 5 is out of support, so current versions are untested. The benchmark repo is small (6 stars, last commit 2021-09-05) and publishes a single BenchmarkDotNet run on one desktop. The complex-POCO schemas are not like-for-like, which inflates Protobuf's complex-deserialize cost: Protobuf stores the child GUID as a string and uses google.protobuf.Timestamp sub-messages and double Percentage/Cost, Bebop uses native guid/date/float32, and MessagePack uses a decimal Cost. On the like-for-like tiny POCO (two int32 fields), Deserialize_Once_TinyPocos still shows BebopStruct 11.93 ns vs Protobuf 85.51 ns (~7.2x, derived). Serialization gains are much smaller, e.g. Serialize_Once_SimplePocos BebopMessage 94.40 ns vs Protobuf 100.82 ns (~1.07x) and Serialize_Once_ComplexPocos BebopStruct 239.2 ns vs Protobuf 926.5 ns (~3.9x) (derived). Bebop's serialize allocates more than both baselines: 1,032 B for complex serialize-once BebopStruct vs 400 B for Protobuf and 304 B for MessagePack. Bebop's own README claims ~10x over Protobuf in C# and TypeScript, but shows only a chart image.

name: hpp-proto
workload: Google Benchmark (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp) runs deserialize, set_message, serialize-only and set_message+serialize. It uses GoogleMessage1 (proto2 and proto3) from the protobuf v3.6.0 benchmarks.proto schema, with a single ~220-byte message filled in code by set_message_google, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. There is also a 'big' variant with 512- and 2048-byte strings, and a 1000-element packed repeated uint64 message with random values. Google protobuf runs in regular and arena modes; hpp-proto runs in regular and non-owning modes.
claimed_speedup: Linux numbers from the README prose (i9-11950H, gcc 13.3.0, protobuf 33.2). Deserialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 210 ns vs 141 ns (~1.5x), proto3 252 ns vs 160 ns (~1.6x). Deserialize regular: proto2 215 vs 210 ns, proto3 251 vs 212 ns. repeated_packed: google regular 4164 ns vs hpp-proto regular 2624 ns (~1.6x); google arena 4263 ns vs hpp-proto non-owning 2550 ns. Set_message+serialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 186 vs 99.6 ns (~1.9x), proto3 223 vs 121 ns (~1.8x); regular: proto2 185 vs 139 ns, proto3 219 vs 148 ns. Google is faster on serialize-only: proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns, proto3 98.8 vs 102 ns. (Ratios derived from page data.)
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17.0.0 (Mac); gcc 13.3.0 (Linux); Google protobuf 33.2. Optimization flags and build type are not stated for the published results. The ReadMe run command sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; CMakePresets.json has a 'benchmark' preset with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, but it is not tied to the published numbers.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (Mac); 11th Gen Intel Core i9-11950H @ 2.60GHz (Linux)
tradeoffs: Requires C++23 compiler (Clang 19+ / GCC 13+); Google protobuf still wins on pure serialize-only of already-constructed objects; biggest gains require the non-owning/arena mode, which changes ownership semantics vs stock generated protobuf classes
caveats: First-party benchmark. Flags and build type are not stated for the published numbers. The README prose numbers do not exactly match the committed benchmarks/Linux_bench.result. For example, in the raw file repeated_packed takes 3966 ns wall / 3852 ns CPU for google regular (the prose says 4164) and 2650 / 2511 ns for hpp-proto regular (the prose says 2624). The workload is one small in-code GoogleMessage1 plus synthetic packed data, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. Google wins serialize-only (proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns). The headline gains compare hpp-proto non-owning mode with Google arena mode; in regular deserialize mode the gap is small (proto2 215 vs 210 ns). The Mac (M1 Pro) results have the same shape. Only two machines were tested, with no variance reported.

name: qdf (Quick Data Format)
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, MessagePack (wire size); MessagePack and Go encoding/json (encode/decode speed)
workload: Wire size and allocations for batches of realistic structured records (OTLP traces, logs, RTB bids, events, IoT float series) encoded record-for-record by json/msgpack/protobuf/flatbuffers/qdf on the same fixtures, via a reproducible `scripts/compare.sh` benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: Wire size at the qdf_compression tier vs protobuf on 5 batch fixtures: RTB 203,360 vs 327,700 B (-38%), IoT 148,177 vs 207,562 B (-29%), OTLP 179,181 vs 561,860 B (-68%), Logs 62,149 vs 156,479 B (-60%), Events 39,639 vs 64,978 B (-39%), i.e. up to 68% smaller than Protobuf. On a 5,000-user Active-Directory export, qdf OptBalanced gives 1,830 KB, 6.6 ms encode and 7.9 ms decode, against encoding/json at 3,833 KB / 14.1 ms / 57.8 ms and msgpack at 3,370 KB / 8.7 ms / 16.7 ms. The page's summary: 2.1x smaller and 2.1x faster encode than json, ~7x faster decode than json, and 1.8x smaller with ~2x faster decode than msgpack. qdf is not faster than protobuf or FlatBuffers. Per the page, protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput and FlatBuffers wins encode allocation outright. Protobuf wins single-tiny-message size and max encode throughput. qdf_balanced and qdf_compression do not win on allocation, though qdf_speed allocates less than protobuf on 4 of 5 fixtures.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 gc toolchain (docs/BENCH.md: Go 1.26.0), default build. scripts/compare.sh runs `go test -run='^$' -bench='RTB|IoT|OTLP|Logs|Events' -benchmem -count=6` in bench/ plus `EMIT_MEM=1 go test -run=TestMemoryReport`. go.mod and bench/go.mod now require go 1.27.0, so the published 2026-06-01 numbers predate the current modules.
hardware: Intel Core i7-9750H @ 2.6 GHz, darwin/amd64 (laptop)
tradeoffs: Go-only, pure-Go, no schema/IDL (struct-tag based, alpha format that 'still moves'). Wins are on batches with cross-record repetition; single tiny messages favor Protobuf/FlatBuffers per author's own comparison. Compression tier trades encode CPU for size (e.g. ~70 MB/s vs ~1100 MB/s for the balanced tier on float data).
caveats: The project is alpha and pre-1.0, and its wire format is still changing. It has 26 stars and was created 2026-05-24. Against Protobuf the win is wire size, not speed: the page concedes that protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput. Speed numbers come from a single i7-9750H laptop run dated 2026-06-01 on Go 1.26, and the author notes they are machine-specific. The AD-export encoding/json and msgpack timings have no public harness for the competitor side, because bench/realistic_ad_test.go and bench/realistic_ad_bench_test.go time only qdf. The README now quotes different figures: ≈6x faster decode than JSON and ~1.5x faster than msgpack on AD, and -24 to -77% wire vs protobuf on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest. Reproducible qdf vs msgpack/json speed tables are in docs/BENCH.md (bench/profiles_test.go, Go 1.26.0, i7-9750H). qdf_compression encode is slow, about 70 MB/s on the IoT float batch.

name: Quarry
workload: Encode/decode ops-per-second and bytes-per-record for telemetry and large-payload workloads, comparing Quarry's C and C++ generated code (BRF wire format) against protoc-generated Protobuf C++ (default and Arena) code, five aggregated CI runs.
claimed_speedup: Results are mixed. The README table is from commit 04349e57, medians of 5 CI runs, in ops/s. Protobuf C++ wins telemetry encode (18.81M vs Quarry C 9.69M), telemetry decode (13.48M vs 5.45M) and large encode (1.60M vs 0.48M). Quarry C wins large decode: 0.85M vs 0.57M for Protobuf C++ (~1.5x) and 0.45M for Protobuf Arena (~1.9x). It also beats Protobuf Arena on large encode, 0.48M vs 0.37M (~1.3x) (ratios derived from page data). Quarry C++ is slower than Protobuf C++ in every row. BRF is larger on the wire: 60 vs 16 bytes/record for telemetry and 1,661 vs 1,425 for large.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (`c++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0`), CMake preset docker-benchmark with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's GCC Release default: -O3 -DNDEBUG). The project builds as C++20 and the Quarry C harness as C99, in an Ubuntu 24.04 dev container. Protobuf/protoc 3.21.12 (libprotoc 3.21.12).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, Linux x86_64, GitHub-hosted runner (docker compose dev container)
tradeoffs: Header-only/deterministic-footprint native runtime (claimed zero native runtime size) vs Protobuf's external runtime library. Larger wire format than Protobuf on tested workloads. Very new/low-adoption project; README explicitly warns shared-runner timing is 'informational' and depends on hardware/compiler/optimization/runtime/workload.
caveats: The project has 4 stars and a single maintainer. It was created 2026-06-19 and is pre-1.0 (v0.1.30-rc.3). The author says the suite 'does not rank backends' and calls the ownership differences 'not a backend-quality ranking'. Quarry C decodes into a caller-owned fixed-capacity struct with no heap allocation, while Protobuf C++ allocates a fresh owning message per decode, so the large-decode win mostly reflects the API model. Shared GitHub-hosted runners add noise. Protobuf 3.21.12 is the Ubuntu distro build, not current Protobuf. Numbers move between commits. The CI artifact for HEAD 5c8adcde (2026-09-20) has Quarry C ahead of Protobuf C++ on large decode (1.17M vs 0.574M ops/s, ~2.0x), nested decode (2.84M vs 1.76M, ~1.6x), large round-trip (~1.6x), nested round-trip (~1.3x) and configuration encode (~1.09x). The same artifact has it behind on telemetry, stress, configuration decode and large/nested encode (ratios derived from artifact data). CI artifacts expire, so the README table is the stable reference.

name: rkyv
baseline: Cap'n Proto, FlatBuffers, Protocol Buffers (via prost/protobuf crates), MessagePack (via rmp-serde/msgpacker/zerompk)
workload: Criterion benchmarks in rust_serialization_benchmark on four Rust datasets: log (HTTP request logs), mesh (triangle mesh), minecraft_savedata (Minecraft player saves) and mk48 (mk48.io game updates). They measure serialize, deserialize, zero-copy access, read and update times, plus encoded size and compressed size. The baselines are Rust crates: capnp 0.27.0, flatbuffers 25.12.19, prost 0.14.4, protobuf 3.7.2 and 4.36.1, rmp-serde 1.3.1, msgpacker 0.7.1 and zerompk 0.8.0.
claimed_speedup: On the 'log' dataset (page run 2026-09-10), rkyv serializes in 178.87 µs, against 763.63 µs for FlatBuffers (~4.3x, derived from page data), 480.15 µs for Cap'n Proto (~2.7x, derived from page data), 731.23 µs for prost encode and 1.3179 ms for rmp-serde. Unvalidated zero-copy access takes 1.0907 ns against 2.1807 ns for FlatBuffers. Unvalidated read takes 8.3309 µs against 42.209 µs for FlatBuffers; the record's '8.33 µs deserialize' was this read figure. rkyv's full unvalidated deserialize takes 1.2188 ms, against 2.6802 ms for prost decode and 2.3829 ms for rmp-serde. rkyv serialize also beats all four baselines on the other datasets: mesh 141.74 µs (FlatBuffers 371.26 µs), minecraft_savedata 212.50 µs (Cap'n Proto 392.46 µs) and mk48 798.81 µs (Cap'n Proto 2.1159 ms). It is not the fastest Rust crate overall. Its serialize speed relative to the best crate is 54.13% (log), 100% (mesh), 38.61% (minecraft_savedata) and 64.85% (mk48). bitcode leads on log and minecraft_savedata.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100.0-nightly (a36d05efa 2026-09-09), LLVM 23.1.1. `cargo bench` runs with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' (tools/bencher/src/main.rs). Cargo.toml sets [profile.bench] lto = true; opt-level 3 is inherited from release. Criterion harness.
hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs (2 cores x 2 threads), on a Microsoft Hyper-V VM (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner), x86_64
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no official C API, so not directly usable from C++ (qualifies under the 'non-C++ implementations welcome' rule). Zero-copy access model requires careful handling of untrusted input (validation feature adds cost, shown separately in the 'validated upfront with error' benchmark rows). Not a schema/IDL system like Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers/Protobuf — Rust-type-driven instead.
caveats: The benchmark repo (rust_serialization_benchmark) is maintained by rkyv's author (djkoloski) with other volunteers, so it is not fully independent. It is public, reproducible and covers about 27 crates. The baselines are the Rust implementations of each format (capnp, flatbuffers, prost/protobuf, rmp-serde crates), not the C++ reference libraries. Relative performance varies by dataset.

name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field out of an already-serialized buffer, for flat messages (10/100 uint64 fields) and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (~2KB working set) and cold (~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Flat Layout reads are ~25-50x faster than Protobuf and ~2-2.5x faster than FlatBuffers on flat messages (e.g. 100-field flat read: 25.99ns YaFF vs 1383.74ns Protobuf vs 54.81ns FlatBuffers); hierarchical hot access is ~25x faster than Protobuf and ~3.5x faster than FlatBuffers
compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, CMake Release build (CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG; no -march or other extra flags in the benchmark CMakeLists), C++20; google/benchmark 1.9.5, FlatBuffers 24.12.23, Protobuf >=5.26 via Conan (the exact Protobuf version is not stated)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7713, x86-64
tradeoffs: Still requires an existing .proto schema (built as a companion physical layout for Protobuf, not a schema replacement); adds adaptive-layout complexity; C++ only today, multi-language bindings are roadmap items

name: JSON BinPack
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers)
workload: Encoded size of 27 real-world JSON documents from SchemaStore, measured uncompressed and after GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 and LZMA -9. There is one document per JSON Taxonomy class (tier x type x redundancy x structure), and each is encoded with JSON BinPack (schema-driven and schema-less) and 13 other formats. JSON BinPack was run through the TypeScript proof of concept (npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x), not the C++ code in this repo.
claimed_speedup: This is a size result only; nothing is claimed about speed. In all 27 documents, JSON BinPack (schema-driven) produced the smallest or tied-smallest uncompressed encoding. The comparison covered Protocol Buffers (Python protobuf 3.12.4), FlatBuffers (flatc 1.12.0), Cap'n Proto 0.7.0 (binary and packed), MessagePack (Python msgpack 1.0.0), Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers and JSON. On four documents it ties with Avro and/or Protocol Buffers. Example: the ESLint configuration encodes to 64 bytes against 1,141 bytes of JSON (~94.4% smaller, derived from page data). Across the 27 documents the median reduction against JSON is ~86.8% and the mean ~78.8% (derived from page data; arXiv 2211.12799 reports 86.7% and 78.7%). The schema-driven uncompressed output is smaller than JSON compressed with GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 or LZMA -9 in all 27 documents (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed (AGPL-3.0-or-later or paid commercial license) — AGPL's network-copyleft is a real adoption barrier for closed-source SaaS use. Space-efficiency focused, not runtime-efficiency focused; project's own FAQ recommends FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto instead when zero-copy runtime speed matters. Requires JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions for schema-driven mode.
caveats: The win is size, not speed. The README concedes runtime efficiency and recommends FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto for extreme runtime efficiency or zero-copy use. The benchmark covers 27 documents; the '400+ SchemaStore documents' figure comes from arXiv 2201.03051, which does not include JSON BinPack. The benchmark ran the archived TypeScript proof of concept (jviotti/jsonbinpack-poc, npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x, February 2022; the page lists 1.1.1 and the Dockerfile installs 1.1.2). The current C++ implementation in this repo is not measured, and the wire format may have changed since. The benchmark is first-party, by the project's author, and the arXiv write-ups are preprints, not peer-reviewed. The README says the MSc dissertation won the 2022 CAR Hoare Prizes. The competitors are older versions (protobuf 3.12.4, flatc 1.12.0, Cap'n Proto 0.7.0). No compiler or hardware is stated, which is irrelevant for byte counts. name: Mison (speculative structural-index JSON parser)
workload: Single-threaded field-projection queries over real-world JSON loaded into memory: Twitter Q1-Q8 (records have 25-30 top-level fields and a nested user object of 37-38 fields), Yelp business records (16 top-level fields), and GitHub user records (31 fixed fields). The paper compares parsing throughput (GB/s) of Mison against Gson, Jackson and RapidJSON, each using its streaming-mode API. It also runs TPC-H queries through Spark with Mison vs Jackson.
claimed_speedup: Paper Sec 6.1.1 / Fig. 8 (Twitter, Q1-Q8, single thread, throughput in GB/s): 'Mison is between 5.5 and 9.1 times faster than the best competitor in this experiment. The best case for Mison (8~9X) is for simple queries on mandatory fields (Q1-Q4)'. RapidJSON is one of the three competitors, so Mison is at least 5.5x faster than RapidJSON on Q1-Q8 (derived from page data; in the Fig. 8 bars Jackson, not RapidJSON, is the best competitor). Sec 6.1.2 (Fig. 9, GitHub dataset, all 31 fields, no projection push-down): Mison 'still outperforms the best existing JSON parser (Jackson) by a factor of 2'. Sec 6.1.4 / Fig. 11 (Twitter, first+last field query): basic (non-speculative) Mison beats Jackson by 3.6x, speculative Mison by 10.2x.
compiler_and_flags: Mison is a C++ static library; the first structural-index step uses 256-bit AVX2 SIMD and the bit-parallel steps use 64-bit instructions. The paper does not state the compiler, its version, or the flags for Mison or RapidJSON, nor the JVM version used for Jackson and Gson.
hardware: 3.5GHz Intel Xeon E5-1620 v3 (the paper calls it 'Broadwell-EP'), 16GB DDR3, 64-bit Windows 10; single-threaded runs with the JSON data preloaded into memory (I/O excluded)
stars_or_usage: Published VLDB 2017 (PVLDB Vol. 10, No. 10, pp. 1118-1129) by Microsoft Research and University of Pittsburgh; no official source release found
tradeoffs: Requires an offline training phase to build 'pattern trees' from sample data before speculative parsing works well; benefit shrinks as the fraction of queried fields grows (Fig. 12) and for highly irregular/schema-varying JSON; only helps analytical/partial-field workloads, not full-document parse+build (Sec 6.1, 'if all fields are needed... [binary formats are] still the most efficient approach').
caveats: No official Mison source was found: the MSR publication page and the paper link no code or artifact. Only unofficial reimplementations exist, none benchmarked against the paper: pikkr/pikkr (Rust, 641 stars, MIT), ubnt-intrepid/misosoup (Rust, 9 stars), leocassarani/mison (Rust, 10 stars, no license), Anghagaed/MISON (21 stars, no license) and indiependente/gomison (Go, 0 stars). The compiler and flags are unstated, and in Fig. 8 RapidJSON (SAX/streaming API on Windows) is slower than Java's Jackson, so the C++ comparison point may not be well tuned. The paper calls the E5-1620 v3 'Broadwell-EP', but v3 Xeon E5 parts are Haswell-EP (a 2014-era CPU). The speedups rely on projection/filter push-down; when all fields are parsed the gain drops to about 2x over Jackson.

name: RapidXml
workload: DOM parse (bemayer/xml-benchmark: 14 libraries across 7 languages, 12 with DOM rows). Each bucket averages a synthetic wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. Every library runs in its own debian:bookworm-slim Docker container on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, with /usr/bin/time capturing RSS and CPU. The 1KB-100MB size labels are only nominal. Because generate_data.py indents every level, the deep files are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label), with 1,706 to 5,000 nesting levels. Only averages across the two shapes are published.
claimed_speedup: bemayer/xml-benchmark DOM Parse, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). RapidXML vs libxml2 throughput: 1084.9 vs 278.8 MB/s in the 10MB bucket (26.93 vs 104.783 ms, ~3.9x, derived from page data); 638.2 vs 161.2 MB/s in the 100MB bucket (163.388 vs 646.685 ms, ~4.0x, derived from page data); 989.0 vs 79.1 MB/s in the 1KB bucket (~12.5x, derived from page data, but at 0.001 vs 0.013 ms, near timer resolution). libxml2 shows higher throughput in the 100KB bucket (3277.1 vs 2017.2 MB/s) and the 1MB bucket (2265.9 vs 1212.7 MB/s). Those buckets include deep files that libxml2 stops parsing partway through (see caveats). pugixml beats RapidXML in every bucket (e.g. 1575.1 vs 1084.9 MB/s at 10MB).
compiler_and_flags: g++ from the debian:bookworm-slim image (bookworm's g++ is 12.2.0; the suite never prints the version). The Dockerfile runs cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's default GCC Release flags are -O3 -DNDEBUG), and benchmarks/rapidxml/CMakeLists.txt adds CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 and -fpermissive. RapidXml is the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip. libxml2 is Debian's prebuilt package (bookworm: 2.9.14), built with the same Release setup.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, with each library in a debian:bookworm-slim Docker container (CPU model not published)
is_fork_of: https://sourceforge.net/projects/rapidxml (not a GitHub fork: externpro/rapidxml imports the upstream RapidXml 1.0-1.13 releases by Marcin Kalicinski and adds CMake/externpro packaging)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars on externpro/rapidxml, a CMake-packaged mirror. Upstream RapidXml's SourceForge page showed '3,065 This Week' downloads on 2026-09-25. bemayer/xml-benchmark uses the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip as its RapidXML entry. The verifier did not check the SpeedyXml-cpp mention.
tradeoffs: In-situ, destructive parser (mutates the source buffer); allocates DOM nodes from an internal per-instance pool, which becomes a scaling bottleneck at large file sizes versus newer arena/SoA designs (see libsimdxml and parshred entries, both of which cite this exact weakness); C++03-era single-header code with no active upstream maintainer since the 1.13 release (2009); canonical home is SourceForge (http://rapidxml.sourceforge.net/), this GitHub repo is a maintained third-party host of the original source
caveats: Only evidence is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It benchmarks the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip, not this repo, though the parser code is the same 1.13. Its size buckets are misleading: deep-shape files are 5.6-100 MiB with up to 5,000 nesting levels. libxml2 2.9.14 (Debian bookworm) stops at depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c nodePush calls xmlHaltParser). The libxml2 bench calls xmlParseMemory without checking the result, so its deep-file times measure a halted partial parse. This favors libxml2, so the ~3.9-4.0x RapidXml win at 10MB/100MB is if anything conservative. The 'libxml2 faster at 100KB/1MB' result is probably this artifact. Per-shape numbers are not published. The run is a single monthly run on a CI runner with no CPU model. RapidXml loses to pugixml at every size, so cite only libxml2 as the beaten baseline. RapidXml is a non-validating in-situ parser, while libxml2 builds a full DOM. The upstream parser has had no release since 1.13 (header dated 2009; SourceForge last updated 2013-04-26). externpro's recent commits (last 2026-08-31) are CMake/CI packaging only, so 'active' reflects packaging, not parser development.

name: PipeYAML
workload: Load/Dump/Roundtrip/Build-sequence/Build-map microbenchmarks (Google Benchmark) on medium (~75 line), complex (anchors/aliases), and deeply-nested YAML documents, plus cached scalar type conversion, comparing against yaml-cpp 0.8
claimed_speedup: Load: 9.4x-10.5x faster (e.g. 14.3us vs yaml-cpp's 150us on a medium document); Dump: 5.0x-5.3x faster; Roundtrip (load->modify->dump): 7.5x faster; cached int/double conversion: 34x/54x faster
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4, C++17, Google Benchmark (README). Optimization flags are not stated. CMakeLists.txt sets no default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and the README build is plain 'cmake ..'. yaml-cpp 0.8 is linked from a prebuilt YAML_CPP_DIR whose build type is also unstated.
hardware: "Intel Xeon" (no specific model number given)
tradeoffs: Type-conversion caching (int/double/bool cached on first access, O(1) subsequent reads) trades a bit of memory/complexity for large gains on repeated field access; API intentionally mirrors yaml-cpp's Node interface for easy migration
caveats: The repo description says the code was written by AI ('本项目代码由AI编写'), and commits are co-authored by an AI tool. The benchmark table was added in commit f1904fc (2026-07-07) and never re-run. Later commits fixed major correctness bugs: flow-parsing infinite loops (07-12), and on 09-08 comments that crashed or truncated parsing, sibling keys swallowed into nested maps, and missing block-scalar support. One known flow-map defect remains. Inputs are tiny (4.5-15 µs parses of a ~75-line config). The 34x/54x 'cached' conversions measure PipeYAML caching repeated as<T>() calls on the same node, which yaml-cpp does not do; they are not parse speedups, and 54x with unstated flags is above the >50x cap. The CPU is the generic 'Intel Xeon' with no model. 0 stars, created 2026-07-03, with no external review or adoption yet.

name: SpeedyXml (SpeedyXml-cpp)
workload: Single-core, streaming SAX-style push parse of a 235 MiB real-world XML document, comparing wall-clock time against pugixml (DOM), RapidXml (in-situ DOM), libxml2 (SAX2 streaming), and Expat (streaming); repeated across 8 additional public XML datasets via a bundled script
claimed_speedup: README table, 235 MiB real-world document, single core: SpeedyXml 0.34 s vs libxml2 (streaming SAX2) 1.53 s (4.4x), pugixml DOM 1.00 s (2.9x), RapidXml DOM in-situ 1.29 s (3.7x), Expat 4.38 s (12.7x); 'That is ~680 MiB/s'. README chart over 8 public datasets ('no other parser reaches half of SpeedyXml's throughput on any document') puts libxml2 at 6-29% of SpeedyXml's throughput, i.e. roughly 3.4x-17x slower (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the published results; tools/public_bench.sh builds the bench tool with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and the system default compiler.
hardware: Not stated
tradeoffs: Streaming SAX-like push model only, not a DOM (caller must build any tree themselves); does not support XML entity declarations with internal DTD subsets, no namespace resolution, UTF-8-only, requires a little-endian machine
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or flags are given for the README numbers, and the 235 MiB document is unnamed and not published (the 8 public datasets in the chart are reproducible via tools/public_bench.sh). The bench tool times each parser once per run with gettimeofday wall clock, in a fixed order with SpeedyXml last. The pugixml/RapidXml rows are DOM vs streaming, as the author notes. The libxml2 comparison is streaming vs streaming, but SpeedyXml does less work: UTF-8 only, no namespace resolution, no DTD entities, not validating, text entities not decoded. Very new (created 2026-07-27), 1-star project with no third-party corroboration.
